column2: Two Black students and a Black teacher from Fisk visit the college; after debate, they are housed in the ordinary dormitories, without incident. Predictions of dire consequences do not come true. Consequences: Serves Foreman as an argument for integration.

Foreman argues that no respectable American citizen or institution can accept intimidation as a guide, that the community must aim at the highest standards in the country, and that the Rosenwald Fund has already offered to subsidize Black students. A financial offer from the Rosenwald Fund. Consequences: Strengthens the convinced without converting the others.

Straus accuses de Graaff in a corridor of using underhanded methods to propagandize the students; she brings the matter to a meeting, where he repeats the accusation. Radin and Bentley come to her defense; Lowinsky and Hansgirg follow; several hours later, twenty shaken people come out without a resolution. 20 people; leaving at night after several hours. Consequences: Reveals the tangle of racial, ideological, and personal questions.

After her colleagues' note asking her to leave, de Graaff lets it be known that she regrets their opinion but believes it is in the college's interest that she stay; she refuses to resign voluntarily and demands that her opponents formulate precise charges and then formally request her resignation. Consequences: Sets off the meetings of the Board of Fellows

The Board of Fellows holds three weeks of meetings on the de Graaff case, summoning her twice; she discovers no concrete charge: no criticism of her teaching, nor of her political or religious views, nor of any misconduct — only that she is supposedly too soft on students and defends them at faculty meetings. 3 weeks of meetings; 2 summonses of de Graaff Consequences: Exasperation on both sides

The effort to keep the family quarrel away from the summer institute people (who see Black Mountain as a Garden of Eden) fails: the two factions sit on opposite sides of the dining hall and walk down opposite sides of the road to avoid each other. Consequences: The conflict becomes visible to the summer visitors

The summer visitor de Creeft, fond of people in both camps, dreams up a way to play out the anger: he organizes a “bullfight,” indiscriminately casting the antagonists as toreadors, picadors, and so on. No perceptible drop in tension. Consequences: The mediation fails

At a faculty meeting, Miller accuses Bentley of using his influence to get certain students to change their field of study; the “intellectual” students had moved from their former advisers to Bentley, de Graaff, and (to a lesser extent) Clark Foreman, wounding the former advisers. Consequences: The former advisers' resentment

The custom was to read aloud letters from former students in military service; Bentley, a baiting leader by his own account, chooses a letter from a former student describing a day in camp and studded with obscenities, then asks Fran to read it without warning her: her imperfect English does not understand these words, and she recites them in a neutral tone. The students roar, the faculty's faces freeze. She afterward pours out explanations to Wunsch and others. The line quoted: “my general said, 'What the fuck are you doin'?!” Consequences: Damages de Graaff's reputation: it was not good for her reputation, she says

At an evening of skits, Bentley imitates Neville Chamberlain and the royal family, stressing George VI's stammer; Straus judges the act, coming from a British subject in wartime, to be in utterly bad taste — which delights Bentley. Consequences: Irritation in the German camp

Bentley reads Brecht to the community, thinking that anti-Hitler refugees would appreciate him; apart from Fritz Cohen, no one knows Brecht; the acid portraits of the bourgeoisie exasperate Hansgirg and Straus, who explains that Brecht's views are entirely incorrect. Frozen looks. Consequences: Bentley's growing isolation

A costume ball on a Surrealist theme whose avowed purpose, for Bentley, was to shock Erwin Straus while exciting him: Janey Stone arrives with an inscription on her crotch, “Abandon hope all ye who enter here”; a woman as a sheaf of wheat bearing “reap me”; another with oil cans tied to her breasts; three students as the Holy Trinity sitting up above; Jeanne Wacker as a bare-chested “hula” girl. The Hansgirgs come dressed as each other. Albers wears a superbly pressed salt-and-pepper tweed with truncated paper cones in front of his eyes; finding the others' choices out of place, he leaves the ball red with anger, on his high horse. Inscriptions, oil cans, paper cones, a salt-and-pepper tweed suit Consequences: Albers and part of the faculty leave in fury

Two months before the Anderson-Wacker episode, the Bentleyites laugh openly at Wunsch's production of Outward Bound, calling it impossibly sentimental and a major disgrace to the college; Wunsch is deeply and dangerously wounded: his central function, his justification for existing, are threatened. 2 months before the Anderson-Wacker episode Consequences: Wunsch's accumulated, repressed resentment

An event mentioned as a landmark (two months after the mockery of Outward Bound); Bentley, Anderson, and Wacker later spoke to Duberman with regret about their sometimes insensitive exuberance, whereas the opposing camp presented itself as blameless, rejecting all responsibility — which strengthened Duberman's sympathy for the Bentleyites. Consequences: The historian's judgment reinforced

Two Board meetings to which de Graaff is summoned to hear her fate deliberated. She tries to obtain the precise list of charges, but none can be agreed upon: one is mentioned, and someone else says, oh no, that is not it at all. The Board invokes vague incompatibilities or trivia such as laundry hung in the public restroom of the Studies Building. A precise charge: Fran hangs her laundry in the public restroom, shocking visitors; she replies that on the salary she is paid she cannot afford underwear pretty enough to be put on display Consequences: No precise charge can be formulated

After the return of Bentley (from Fisk) and Foreman (from work for the C.I.O.), and their protest, with the Cohens, against Fran's treatment, the Board broadens its charge: Bentley and de Graaff are named as the two members whose views are so at odds with the essential aims of the College that working with them is no longer possible. Consequences: Foreman and the Cohens offer their resignations in protest

De Graaff resigns first, preparing a formal statement denouncing a case dishonestly framed against her and Bentley. She accepts the Board's offer (conditional on her voluntary resignation) to guarantee her 1000 dollars the following year if she finds no job. Immediately afterward, Bentley, the Cohens, and Foreman also decline reelection. 1000 dollars guaranteed for the following year; Elsa Kahl Cohen resigns specifically out of lack of respect for the faculty and disappointment at its actions; the Cohens are particularly bitter that the Board refuses to wait until the end of the summer Music Institute, for which Fritz Cohen has worked so hard Consequences: The college splits for good into two camps

Immediately after the resignation of de Graaff (who was guaranteed a thousand dollars the following year if she found no job), Bentley, the Cohens, and Clark Foreman decline reelection; Elsa Kahl Cohen cites her lack of respect for the faculty and her disappointment at its actions. a guarantee of 1000 dollars for the following year Consequences: a third of the college, including almost all the young teachers, leaves

Jalowetz, disgusted with all the belligerents but above all with the old guard, writes to the Board asking to be relieved of his duties on it; for the first time his loyalty to Black Mountain is shaken and he starts looking for other work. The Jalowetzes stay, but declare that their sympathy lies with Bentley and de Graaff and that they would leave too if they were not too old and had somewhere else to go. Consequences: foreshadows his death from heart failure a year later

A few days after the teachers' resignations, the student Moderator and all the student officers resign; eleven students (the number will rise to twenty) sign a statement announcing their departure in protest: the purge disguised as pedagogical differences reveals the supreme intolerance of theory against practice. 11, then 20 student signers Consequences: a counterstatement by an equivalent group of music and art students expressing their confidence in the college

Wunsch, as rector, sends parents, alumni, and the Advisory Council an explanation full of platitudes; the student officers send their own account, reproaching Wunsch for his phrase about seeking a solution without de Graaff's departure (withdrawing the letter of the ten was never considered) and noting that five signers of that letter made up the majority of the nine-member Board of Fellows — judges in their own cause. 5 signers on a Board of 9 Consequences: John Evarts, in the military overseas, receives the batch of contradictory statements plus two private letters from Wunsch

Wunsch blames the intrigue of the young teachers and articulate students, above all Bentley and Foreman, determined either to control the college entirely or to destroy it; he confesses that de Graaff has been the scapegoat, but reproaches her for having become more a female than a woman in her infatuation with Bentley. Consequences: Evarts is not fooled: he replies that Wunsch's report says practically nothing in a roundabout way

Evarts writes to Wunsch that his report was like a funeral notice; he thinks the Board was wrong about Fran and shudders at the weight thrown in by the Alberses, the Hansgirgs, the Strauses, and that sturdy conservative Mr. Lowinsky; he does not miss Bentley or Foreman, but very much misses the Cohens and Frances: the mixture did not take — the influx of novelty was too strong a dose.

An alumnus, visiting the college when the conflict erupted, recalls the crisis over John Rice: the ultimatum then was either he goes or we go; now it is simply you go; no one handled the situation in the “Black Mountain Way” of old.

When de Graaff leaves, Wunsch writes that most of them hated to see her go — while adding that very few would want to see her come back. Those who remain hold late meetings to clarify the aims; the report to the alumni lists all the causes put forward for the split without settling on any, then suddenly decides in favor of differences of educational orientation. Weariness and depression become endemic; Albers shows his impatience with Straus's antimodernism; Kurtz develops a sharp dislike of Dreier, who is so exhausted that he is persuaded to take a vacation. a student remembers Dreier's shattered nerves: he could barely finish a sentence Consequences: the college has fallen back on a supposed need for consensus

De Graaff stays briefly with Barbara Anderson and Jeanne Wacker in an apartment in Greenwich Village, then moves with the Cohens into a small house rented by the Foremans on Park Avenue. Foreman knows of a half-built, abandoned hotel that could house a new college and is looking for funding. In the meantime, de Graaff works for the Office of War Information, Elsa Cohen compiles a Russian-English dictionary for the Army Service Groups; Fritz Cohen finds no job equal to his abilities and pins his hopes on the new college.

Bentley spends a few months at the Kenyon Review (a fellowship combined with a small job), then obtains a post at the University of Minnesota — which his opponents read as proof that his first loyalty was to his career. De Graaff, who had never believed 100 percent in the new college, teaches for two years at Wells and then at Bryn Mawr.

George, the cook, strikes the big triangle to call people to breakfast around 6:30 a.m.; Peggy Bennett Cole remembers that he probably played his noisy instrument twice, first around 6 a.m. to wake people up, then at 6:30 for the call. Triangle struck at ~6 a.m., then 6:30; breakfast around 6:30 a.m.

On Peggy Bennett Cole's very first evening, after the meal, the room bursts spontaneously into song: one table strikes up the first verse of “Green Grow the Rushes, Ho!”, then falls silent and waits; a second table answers joyfully, then a third, and so on until the song is exhausted. The song “Green Grow the Rushes, Ho!”, sung by the tables in turn

On Peggy Bennett Cole's first evening (or nearly), Ted Dreier taps his water glass with a table knife for silence and announces that “Jalo” and Eddie Lowinsky have prepared an evening of music; greeted with ohs and ahs and applause. Lowinsky is a good pianist but seems to have had only that role at concerts, while Jalowetz conducted the ensembles and also played the piano. A water glass tapped with a table knife

After the 1944 split and the departures (Kurtz and Straus on leave), the college no longer has a biologist, an economist, a historian, a psychologist, or a language teacher. Mrs. Hansgirg gives French lessons; Lowinsky a course on Renaissance culture standing in for a history course. The college gets by because most of the 1944-1945 students are new and are encouraged to concentrate on the college “in the making” rather than on its past. Consequences: Progressive rhetoric coincides with the need to avoid defeatism.

The Board of Fellows sets up the beginnings of a retirement system: $300 a year in government bonds for the three teachers aged at least fifty with five years of service. Consequences: Material for the 1949 quarrel.

Fritz Cohen proposes his uncle Max Shellens, who has had a long business career, as “Administrator” to replace Bob Orr; his conditions are judged arrogant; Dreier takes over the business office again, which sharpens criticism of his accumulation of powers. Consequences: Dreier back in charge of business affairs

A rumor that Barbara Anderson has gonorrhea; Bentley asserts peremptorily that she did not (not a scientific statement, but the closest thing to divine truth); Bray cites a health certificate issued by an Asheville doctor; no case of gonorrhea is said to have occurred at BMC. A medical certificate from an Asheville doctor Consequences: Barbara's reputation called into question

Lowinsky and Anni Albers are indignant at de Graaff's irresponsibility (the girls having hitchhiked); de Graaff asserts that she warned the girls against hitchhiking; Andy and Jeanne, as far as they remember, confirm it. Hitchhiking
According to de Graaff, Hansgirg nearly fainted (context: the affair of the women students, July 1944).

De Graaff reports two cases of arbitrary fussiness: Albers refuses to pass a student (who did excellently on the second day of the examination) because she does not know whether the beams of the dining hall ceiling run lengthwise or crosswise; then he refuses a boy because he is shabby — intelligent, neat in his work and his room, but poor, with few clothes and no money to have them cleaned. Jalowetz, Cohen, Eric, and de Graaff look at one another and whisper: do you know? None of them does. They protest on the boy's behalf and win.
Photograph taken by Josef Breitenbach showing Josef Albers's color course at Black Mountain College. A black-and-white photograph reproduced in the guide

“The Educational Value of Manual Work and Handicraft in Relationship to Architecture,” in the symposium edited by Paul Zucker, New Architecture and City Planning (Philosophical Library): his most thorough examination of the subject.

Jalowetz organizes a summer music institute in honor of Arnold Schoenberg's 70th birthday, on the theme of “interpretation,” turning Black Mountain into a center of Schoenberg studies. Jalowetz had prepared there a two-piano arrangement of Schoenberg's Ode to Napoleon (1942), an explicitly “anti-Hitler” work. Kulish teaches the course Democratic Practices of Ensemble Playing. Albers invites visual artists: Breitenbach (photography), de Creeft (sculpture), Charlot, Ozenfant, Rudofsky (clothing design, before the invention of the Bernardo sandal). Gropius comes to lecture, as do the directors of education of the Baltimore Museum of Art and MoMA. Schoenberg's 70th birthday; Ode to Napoleon for string quartet, piano, and speaker (1942), Jalowetz's two-piano arrangement Consequences: the beginning of the summer art institutes; an influx of art students

The institute's flagship course, twice a week: a public rehearsal of Schoenberg's String Quartet in D Minor, Op. 7, with the score projected on a screen suspended above the musicians, coordinated with the music, allowing the audience to follow the work-out through conversation and demonstration of the structural function of each musical phenomenon. A projection screen suspended above the performers Consequences: A model of public music teaching

Lotte Leonard leads “Interpretation of Vocal Music,” Marcel Dick “Interpretation of Instrumental Music”; invited American composers: Sessions, Brunswick, Bacon, Nowak; the piano-cello duo Johanna and Nikolai Graudan and the harpsichordist Yella Pessl on the instrumental faculty; the college musicologist Edward Lowinsky leads courses in music history; Agnes de Mille and Doris Humphrey lead round tables on music in dance and theater.
Two murals, Inspiration and Knowledge, painted on the pylons of the Studies Building.

She comes from Milwaukee State Teachers College for the first summer art institute, drawn by a short article in a local newspaper. a local newspaper article as the trigger Consequences: She comes back in 1945 and stays nine years in all

A series of meetings prompted by the new teachers, who feel responsible for the cause of racial equality, brings latent tensions to a boil; the “Negro problem” becomes the pretext for a fear of a coup against Albers and Dreier Wunsch writes to John Evarts (letter of April 20, 1944) that integrating would amount to declaring open war on the South; Clark Foreman draws up lists of the positive and negative effects of integration Consequences: integration efforts continually postponed on the pretext of waiting for the ideal moment for a radical break with Southern procedure

The creation of this piano piece, evoking the turbulence of his failed marriage, is a turning point: Cage realizes that he is not communicating the emotion he has invested. Consequences: Cage decides to give up composing if he does not find a better motive than communication.
Olson and Shahn work together to mobilize ethnic minorities for President Roosevelt's reelection in 1944.
Brochures of the 1944 “Music, Art, and Work Institute” preserved in the Western Regional Archives of North Carolina (8 x 5 inches each). 8 x 5-inch format
A lecture titled “Philosophy of Art” presented during the 1944 summer session at the college (transcript preserved).
A lecture on the philosophy of art given during the 1944 summer session; transcript preserved.

In the mid-1940s, while enrolled at Milwaukee State Teachers' College, Archer discovers Black Mountain College in the Milwaukee newspaper; its experimental educational model matches her aspiration to teach beyond rote learning. Consequences: She applies to the 1944 summer institute.

Archer applies as a student to the 1944 Black Mountain Summer Institute; she credits Josef Albers and her longtime friend Beaumont Newhall as her most influential teachers, and also works with Lyonel Feininger. Consequences: The start of her long relationship with the college.

Professors present to Frank Fackenthal, acting president, a formal ten-point proposal creating the Seminars; five points concern the recruitment and examination of students, and the Seminars are empowered to grant academic credit; proposal 6 provides for their own publications (a Seminar on slavery or on crime, which will never exist). Ten proposals; proposal 6 quoted almost in full Consequences: Against all expectations, the Seminars will gradually exclude students and stop publishing, in favor of dialogue

Expelled from the university after six months for refusing to dissect a frog in anatomy class; shortly afterward, drafted into the Navy. a frog, an anatomy class Consequences: induction into the Navy, basic training at Farragut, Idaho
Located in the segregated South, the college admits Black students from 1944.

Gropius praises Albers's teaching innovation: he does not hand students a ready-made system but objective tools for digging into the stuff of life, a changing approach pregnant with life, present and future.

The college hosts a highly publicized and internationally renowned conference celebrating Schoenberg's 75th birthday — proof that Black Mountain was an outpost of experimental music in the 1930s and 1940s.

Fuller patents a low-distortion projection of the earth that can be folded in several orientations and assembled into a three-dimensional globe; he presents it as a template for displaying networked information (world comparisons of energy, resources, unequal consumption between industrialized and underdeveloped nations) A project first intended for educational distribution in elementary schools; a failure because of prohibitive costs Consequences: An instrument of his vision of “Spaceship Earth”
The cofounder of French Purism paints during his stay an influential series of realist paintings of Black Mountain

Albers creates a chenille drapery fabric with a warp of white plastic and copper Lurex, with fine stripes that sparkle at night and remain calm and discreet by day, for the Rockefeller Guest House. chenille, white plastic, copper Lurex

Sale of “The Metamorphosis of Mr. Cracovaner”; followed by a three-year first-reading agreement giving the New Yorker a right of first refusal on all his short fiction. Consequences: Irregular income but literary recognition.
The Rice family grows to four with Elisabeth's birth in 1944. Consequences: The family lives on a shoestring thanks to one or two stories a year.
The Rice family grows to four with Elisabeth's birth. Consequences: A larger family, income still precarious.

Early in the community debate, the students vote two to one to admit Black students the following term (fall 1944). Result: 2 to 1. Consequences: The faculty splits almost exactly in half on the same question.

For four months, the public debate rages mainly over the Negro question; camps: for admission (Foreman, Bentley, de Graaff, the Cohens, the Jalowetzes, Radin); against (Straus, Anni and Josef Albers, Hansgirg, Kurtz, Wunsch, Gregory, Miller, then, after hesitation, Dreier and Lowinsky). The “for” camp: Foreman, Bentley, de Graaff, the Cohens, the Jalowetzes, Radin. The “against” camp: Straus, the Alberses (Anni and Josef), Hansgirg, Kurtz, Wunsch, Gregory, Miller, Dreier and Lowinsky after hesitation. Consequences: A lasting division of the community.

A series of faculty meetings (January 25, February 1 and 15, April 12, 17, 19, 24, May 3 and 10, 1944) on admitting Black students; Foreman writes a summary of the discussions. Multiple community bulletins (Nos. 22, 26, of March 6 and April 3, 1944) Consequences: The decision to admit a Black woman student

Gretel opens the living room and turns on the light; Eva walks in, screams, jumps onto the coffee table; Gretel removes the little green snake before she will come down Atmosphere: Comic, a star's scream, an after-concert night

While the community tears itself apart, the student sitting at the loom throws the shuttle while looking for her own answers: what to believe? what to live with? The Kolisch Quartet rehearses Schoenberg on the other side of the lake. Atmosphere: cool and silent, an inner earthquake beneath a motionless surface Stakes: a nascent political and moral awareness in the face of adults tearing one another apart

After dinner one Saturday evening, de Creeft organizes a bullfight: Goulet plays the bull, de Creeft the matador; the author, president of the ring in a black cardboard top hat, solemnly orders the fight to begin. Words: the author, very dignified, gives the command to begin; he does not remember awarding any “ears” Atmosphere: an after-dinner burlesque festival

An after-dinner round table on dance in history, a summer storm rolling around the valley. De Mille, forefinger raised, asserts that it was the Church that banned dancing from worship — a deafening clap of thunder cracks instantly: a shiver, a gasp, a delirium of laughter led by de Mille herself. Words: de Mille: it was THE CHURCH that banned dancing in the rituals Atmosphere: the heat of a summer storm, an enormous silence, theatrical lightning, collective hilarity — the forces of nature seemed to be in concert with the discussion Stakes: the sacred bursts into the aesthetic debate

After a good soak in the cast-iron bathtub on lion's feet standing on the bare floor, Sussler dresses for dinner; just below, every afternoon, Sadoff practices the double bass; motionless in the hot water, she imagines the joists vibrating to the thick strings, taking care to make no unnecessary noise. Atmosphere: hot water, wood, a deep resonance rising; a secret, musical intimacy Stakes: an invisible duet between a bather and a musician unaware of each other

The two pianists take their places at the grand pianos in the dining hall for an evening of excerpts from Carmen; student singers come up to sing to their accompaniment; the Habanera, swept along in improvised tempos and extravagant rubatos, brings down the house. Atmosphere: magic, celebration, the house brought down — the audience in raptures

For his birthday, Hansgirg entertains: a Bach trio on piano, cello, and violin; champagne is served with peaches macerated for a week in 100-proof alcohol — after one or two, people float across the lawn; during the concert, two mice come out and dance. Atmosphere: cream-Cadillac elegance, alcoholic giddiness, the involuntary burlesque of the mice

Marion calls out to him to come and see; Coron runs and follows her finger pointing ten yards away under some dwarf pines: a white flower on a long hooded stem — the Oconee bell he had searched for in vain for years. He jumps for joy. Words: Marion: “Come here and see what this is!” Atmosphere: wonder, a lost species found again in his own garden Stakes: the reward of three years of searching

In the middle of the night, a girl knocks at Coron's door: a fellow student is at death's door. The ranger telephones the college; Molly Gregory leaps into her car, fifteen miles of switchback roads, and arrives at 2 a.m.; the next day, she catches Coron to tell him that the sick girl had only drunk too much bootleg “mountain dew”. Words: Molly, relieved and amused, reports the truth the next day Atmosphere: nighttime panic at altitude, then a comic outcome Stakes: the responsibility of teachers on excursions

After a heavy rain, coming out of Meadows Inn, Coron notices in the washed gravel a small, beautifully shaped arrowhead; from then on they leap out of the ground at him, especially in the sloping cornfield. Atmosphere: wet ground, a revelation that changes a life Stakes: the birth of a historian's vocation

De Creeft hands out the roles of toreadors, picadors, and so on, deliberately mixing the antagonists to play out the anger Atmosphere: Surface gaiety, tension intact Stakes: Trying to exorcize hatred through play

Bentley receives a letter from a former student in camp, full of obscenities; he asks Fran to read it aloud without warning her; she reels off the obscenities in a neutral tone, the students roar, the faculty's faces fall; she squirms without understanding; afterward she explains herself to Wunsch Words: “my general said, 'What the fuck are you doin'?!”; Fran: “I don't think they believed it… It wasn't good for my reputation.” Atmosphere: Student hilarity, faculty horror, Fran's humiliation Stakes: Bentley's light cruelty; a discredit that sticks to de Graaff

A Surrealist costume ball: Janey Stone with an inscription on her crotch, a sheaf-of-wheat woman with “reap me,” oil cans on breasts, the Holy Trinity up above, Jeanne Wacker as a bare-chested hula girl; the Hansgirgs dressed as each other; Albers in pressed tweed with paper cones over his eyes; seeing the other costumes, he flushes with anger and walks out on his high horse, followed by other teachers Words: Bentley: “It got the desired rise out of everybody”; the inscription “Abandon hope all ye who enter here” Atmosphere: Provocation, hilarity, scandal, a furious exit Stakes: The climax of the culture war of 1944

Summoned twice in three weeks, she confronts her judges: no concrete charge; only that she is supposedly too soft on students Words: A prepared statement: no criticism of her teaching, nor of her political or religious views, nor of any misconduct — only her softness and her defense of the students Atmosphere: Procedural, mildly Kafkaesque Stakes: The absence of charges delegitimizes her removal

Two Board meetings at which de Graaff tries to obtain precise charges. Each time an accusation is put forward, another member rejects it. The Board brings up incompatibilities or details such as the laundry in the restroom. Words: De Graaff asks for the list of charges. A Board member: oh no, that is not it at all. Fran on the laundry: on the salary she is paid, she cannot afford underwear pretty enough to be hung out. Atmosphere: Kafkaesque, absurd, humiliating Stakes: It is impossible to defend oneself against charges that cannot be formulated

Jalowetz, a man of the middle, unhappy with the controversy, gives a speech at a Board meeting denouncing the logic of autos-da-fé. Words: Jalowetz: we are often told that a community must have a common idea, but what is offered on all sides is ideologies rather than ideas; he always has the impression of autos-da-fé in progress, and he thinks autos-da-fé are necessary only when one is afraid of something. Atmosphere: Sad, despairing, lucid Stakes: The last voice of reason before the final split

The man of the middle speaks: it is said over and over that a community must have a common idea, but all that has poured in is ideologies; he has the impression of autos-da-fé, and autos-da-fé serve only those who are afraid Words: ideologies rather than ideas; the impression of autos-da-fé Atmosphere: an old man's weariness and lucidity Stakes: the voice of wisdom crushed by the camps

On Peggy Bennett Cole's first evening, after the meal, a central table strikes up the first verse of “Green Grow the Rushes, Ho!”, then falls silent and waits; another table answers with gusto, then a third takes over; and so on until the song is exhausted; the new student listens, astounded. Atmosphere: Gladness, glorious abandon, an unexpected tradition Stakes: A newcomer's initiation into community culture

At a magnificent but icy fall dawn, George strikes the big triangle, first around 6 a.m. to wake people up, then at 6:30 to call them to breakfast; few students turn up; among the faculty, Ted Dreier in blue work clothes now and then, Wunsch fairly regularly. Atmosphere: The cold of dawn, a cool and mysterious light, the clamor of the triangle

One day of pouring rain, when the light stays dark, a handful of brave souls arrive dripping in their raincoats, shiny and wet as frogs; they crowd at the corner tables near the kitchen and the windows over the lake, chatting in low voices, laughing and joking. Atmosphere: A rich half-light, the kitchen lights dear and brave, the knowing intimacy of adventurers

Ted Dreier taps his water glass with a table knife to call for silence during dinner and announces that Jalo and Lowinsky have prepared an evening of music; volleys of ohs and ahs and applause. Atmosphere: Joyful anticipation, a thrill of applause

After a successful examination, Albers refuses to pass the student: she does not know whether the ceiling beams run lengthwise or crosswise. Jalowetz, Cohen, Eric, and de Graaff exchange looks and whisper: do you know? None of them does. Words: They ask one another in whispers whether they themselves would know the answer — no. Atmosphere: Ironic stupefaction at the arbitrariness. Stakes: Albers's authority judged absurd by his own colleagues.

At the end of his first summer stay, Gropius praises Albers's teaching: instead of a ready-made formulated system, he gives objective tools for digging into the substance of life and developing independence and constructive ingenuity. Words: He would like to send every student of design or engineering to Albers's courses. Atmosphere: A public tribute from the founder of the Bauhaus to his former colleague. Stakes: Albers's teaching recognized by the highest authority in world design.

The opening of the session: Jalowetz, an exiled former conductor, gives an opening address arguing for the role of music in the stupendous task of rebuilding our shaken world, in tribute to Schoenberg on his 70th birthday. Words: Jalowetz: music must serve “the stupendous task of reconstructing our shaken world” Atmosphere: the solemnity of exiles, music against tyranny Stakes: making art a moral act in the face of Nazism

Albers has identical colored papers placed on different grounds; the students note that their perceptions diverge; exercises in vibration, color change, and materials (cigarette ash as rock). Words: Albers to Rauschenberg: one color is as good as another; believing that one color is better is merely a personal preference Atmosphere: clinical discipline, perceptual astonishment Stakes: unsettling common sense and taste

During a visit, Gropius observes Albers's teaching and salutes it publicly: ready-made systems abandoned in favor of objective tools. Words: he gives them objective tools for digging into the very stuff of life… an ever-changing approach, pregnant with life, present and future. Stakes: The Bauhaus master's recognition of the student turned teacher.

As de Kooning's paintings fill with Picassoesque distortions, Graham comes and sits with his back to the paintings, unable to witness the creative struggle, but repeating his loyalty to his friend. Words: “Bill, whatever you're doing is good enough for me”; he cannot “stand someone struggling” Atmosphere: Uneasy affection, aesthetic misunderstanding Stakes: The loyalty of a mentor turned reactionary in the face of an art he no longer understands
Stephen Duggar Jr. writes to Foreman (January 20, 1944); Wunsch makes his own inquiries (letters to Junius Allison of April 12, June 27, July 17, 1944) and receives the same legal answer.

A student resigns (noted on February 1, 1944); the assistant treasurer, Robert C. Orr, resigns (April 26, 1944), admitting that the admission of a Black woman student partly contributed, but also denouncing BMC's disease: attempting too much with too little. The phrase: the-attempting-of-too-much-with-too-little Consequences: The administrator's post left vacant

Zora Hurston (February 21, 1944) and Rubye Lipsey (February 21, 1944) write to Wunsch; James E. Shepard, president of the North Carolina College for Negroes, writes on March 20, 1944, that the great agitation in the country over the Negro problem would at present make admitting Black students in the fall term do more harm than good. Letter from Wunsch to Effie Mae Drake, February 1, 1944

Early spring: Wunsch proposes admitting one to three carefully chosen Black people, as mere visitors, for three to four weeks at most, during the music institute, preceded by a course on race relations for the whole community. 1 to 3 people, 3-4 weeks at most, visitor status. Consequences: Several more weeks of debate before consensus.

The compromise settles on a single qualified, older Black woman, admitted for the whole summer session with a hybrid status of member of the Institute — Bentley mocks it, speaking of the Hofjude (the court Jew). Straus declares that he remains opposed but will not fight for his opinion. A single person, the status of member of the Institute, neither visitor, nor guest, nor student. Consequences: An official consensus, but the gulf remains.

De Graaff files a complaint about Straus's corridor accusation; Straus repeats it and adds the abuse of democratic institutions; Radin asks from what point a teacher has the right to lose patience; Bentley rages at being accused of communism; Lowinsky needles Bentley; Hansgirg confusedly repeats the accusation while believing he is withdrawing it; Radin defends himself with his own case; after several hours, twenty exhausted people go out into the night with nothing resolved. Words: Straus: she spoke behind closed doors to the students to push them into a certain position. Hansgirg: they must not poison the students' minds with communist propaganda against religion, and so on. Atmosphere: Unbearable tension; the atmosphere was so thick that breathing was painful, says Dreier Stakes: The community tears itself apart over the line between conviction and propaganda

A Black woman, a music teacher at Fort Valley College in Georgia, is accepted as a student; recommended by the historian Horace Mann Bond, father of Julian Bond. Consequences: The first admission of a Black woman to BMC
